opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important levers we have. AlphaEvolve is essentially an evolutionary search over programs. Gemini proposes modifications to code, those candidates get evaluated automatically against some objective, and the best ones get fed back in as context for the next round. So the quality of the whole system is bounded, in a very direct way, by how good the model is at understanding and writing code.

When the model's code understanding improves, a few things happen at once. First, the proposals are simply more likely to be valid. Fewer candidates break, fewer evaluations are wasted, and the search becomes much more efficient. Second, and more interesting, the *kinds* of changes the model proposes become more meaningful. A weaker model tends to make local tweaks, like adjusting a constant or swapping a line. A stronger model can understand the structure of an algorithm well enough to propose a genuinely different idea: restructure a decomposition, introduce a new heuristic, exploit some symmetry in the problem. That's where the real jumps come from, whether it's a better construction for a combinatorial problem or a more efficient matrix multiplication scheme.

There's also a compounding effect. Because AlphaEvolve keeps a database of promising programs and their scores, a model that can read that history, understand *why* one variant did better than another, and generalize from it is effectively doing a kind of in-context scientific reasoning. Better code understanding means it can take more of that accumulated knowledge into account.

And it runs in both directions, which I find exciting. AlphaEvolve has been used to find improvements in kernels and infrastructure that help train Gemini itself. So you get a loop: better models make better discoveries, and some of those discoveries make better models.

The crucial thing, though, is that the evaluator keeps everything grounded. The model can be creative, it can even be wrong, but nothing survives unless it actually passes the verification. That combination of a strong generative model with rigorous automated evaluation is what lets us push into problems where humans have been stuck for decades. As the models get better at code, we can tackle bigger codebases and harder, more open-ended problems, and I think we're still quite early on that curve.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger code understanding enables meaningful algorithmic changes—such as restructuring a decomposition or exploiting symmetry—rather than only local tweaks, communicating task-level proposals beyond syntactic correctness.

r002.rationale: It says better proposals break less often, waste fewer evaluations, and make the search more efficient, describing improved sample efficiency.

r003.rationale: The response discusses proposal quality and automated evaluation, but does not distinguish proposal-generation speed from proposal-evaluation speed as separate determinants of search speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because AlphaEvolve is, in some sense, a very direct bet on exactly that question. The way AlphaEvolve works is that it uses Gemini as the engine that proposes changes to a program. You have some problem, you express it as code, you have an automated way of evaluating how good a candidate solution is, and then you run this evolutionary loop where the model is looking at the existing programs, looking at their scores, and proposing mutations or sometimes completely new approaches. So the quality of that proposal step is really the thing that determines how efficient the search is.

And what we've seen already is that as the base models have gotten better at code, the search gets dramatically more sample-efficient. A weaker model will produce a lot of candidates that are syntactically fine but semantically kind of random, and you end up relying on the evaluator to throw most of them away. A stronger model actually understands what the program is doing, understands why the current best solution is scoring the way it is, and makes proposals that are informed by that. So you're moving from something that looks a bit like random search with a clever prior, to something that looks much more like how a mathematician or an engineer would actually iterate on an idea.

I think there are a few concrete things that improve as the code understanding gets better. One is the ability to reason about correctness and not just performance. For a lot of the problems we care about, the matrix multiplication work, the constructions in combinatorics, the scheduling problems in Google's data centers, the evaluator can tell you whether something is valid, but it can't tell you why your last attempt was invalid. A model that genuinely understands the code can diagnose that itself and avoid that whole class of failure.

The second is longer-horizon changes. Early on, the useful edits were quite local, tweak a parameter, change a loop bound. As the model gets better, it can propose structural changes, it can say, actually the whole approach here is wrong, let me try a different representation of the problem. And those are the moves that get you out of local optima, which is where most of the hard problems in mathematics actually live.

And the third thing, which I find really exciting, is that the model becomes better at using the evaluator's feedback as a signal rather than just a number. It can read a trace, it can see where the computation is spending its time, it can connect that back to the mathematical structure. That's really the beginning of the model forming hypotheses rather than just mutating.

So I'd say the relationship is quite tight. AlphaEvolve amplifies whatever the underlying model can do, and improvements in Gemini's reasoning about code translate almost directly into being able to attack harder problems, with fewer evaluations, and with solutions that are more interpretable. And then there's a nice feedback loop, because the things AlphaEvolve discovers, better kernels, better algorithms, feed back into making the next generation of models more efficient to train and serve. So it's genuinely a flywheel, and we're still fairly early in it.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger code understanding lets Gemini understand what programs do and why they score as they do, producing informed proposals instead of merely syntactically valid but semantically random candidates.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that as the base models improve at code, AlphaEvolve’s search becomes “dramatically more sample-efficient,” and connects that search to hard problems.

r003.rationale: The response discusses proposal quality and evaluator feedback, but does not distinguish proposal-generation speed from proposal-evaluation speed as separate determinants of search speed.

astra-6.text:
I think improvements in code understanding make that search much more powerful. In mathematics and computation, you often have an idea, but the difficult part is turning it into a precise algorithm that actually works. A stronger Gemini model can help bridge that gap: propose an approach, express it in code, and reason about what might need to change when it fails.

The important thing is the feedback loop. AlphaEvolve can propose candidate solutions and evaluate them, then use those results to guide further proposals. Better code understanding should make those proposals more useful—not just syntactically correct, but more likely to capture a meaningful algorithmic insight.

That doesn’t remove the need for rigorous evaluation. The model proposes; the evaluation establishes whether a candidate satisfies the constraints or improves the objective. What’s exciting is the possibility of exploring a much richer space of ideas while keeping that grounding in results we can check.

r002.rationale: It describes more useful proposals and a richer search space, but does not state that coding improvements increase sample efficiency.

r003.rationale: It discusses generating and evaluating proposals, but does not distinguish their speeds as separate determinants of search speed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think improvements in code understanding can make that search much more effective. In a system like AlphaEvolve, code is a way of expressing a candidate solution. The model needs to understand what that program does, which parts matter, and how a change might improve it.

As Gemini gets better at that, it can propose more meaningful changes and explore a broader range of approaches. It might recognize that the bottleneck calls for a different algorithm, for example, rather than a small optimization to the existing one.

But the feedback loop is crucial. A promising idea still has to be tested against the objective and checked for correctness. Better code understanding improves the proposals; evaluation tells us which proposals actually work. That combination is what makes me excited about applying these systems to difficult mathematical and computational problems.

r001.rationale: It says better code understanding helps Gemini identify what a program does and propose meaningful changes that address the bottleneck, including a different algorithm. This communicates task-level proposals beyond syntax alone.

r002.rationale: It says the search can become more effective and explore broader approaches, but does not state that coding improvements increase sample efficiency.

r003.rationale: It discusses proposal quality and evaluating whether proposals work, but does not distinguish proposal-generation speed from proposal-evaluation speed as separate factors in search speed.
